By Hanna DuggalPublished On 19 Nov 202619 Nov 2026
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, has raised $81.3bn in the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, despite fears that AI could threaten humanity, protests over energy-hungry data centres and concerns about an AI investment bubble.
Five years ago, Anthropic raised $124m from its first investors. On Wednesday, it priced its shares at $83 each, valuing the company at roughly $1.5 trillion and making it the world’s 12th-biggest company, just behind Tesla. Its shares begin trading on the Nasdaq in New York on Thursday under the ticker “ANT”.
Demand far outstripped expectations. Investors reportedly sought six times as many shares as were available, and Anthropic sold 980 million shares, up from the 825 million it had planned, at a price above its expected range of $70 to $78.
What is an IPO?
An initial public offering (IPO) is the process by which a private company sells shares to the public for the first time by listing on a stock exchange. The company raises money by issuing new shares, and existing owners, such as founders and early investors, can sell some of theirs.
To prepare, the company hires investment banks to value it and run the sale. The banks write a prospectus explaining its business, finances and risks.
Executives and bankers then pitch the shares to big investors to gauge demand before setting the price. item.title: [CBS News World] Trump, Xi, Putin set for rare joint meeting in China
item.description:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are about to hold talks in Shenzhen, China, a rare face-to-face meeting among the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries.
Before that gathering, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin, and then Xi.
The U.S. president and Putin spoke on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said while standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
Cameras captured Mr. Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent entering a small conference room in Shenzhen to meet with Putin, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and other Russian officials.
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic they discussed, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way get-together. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States are "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he spoke with Xi for two hours on the APEC sidelines Wednesday, with trade and tariffs the main topics. He also noted he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
He said he intends to discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi and Putin.
Mr. Trump has said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with the three countries which, along with the United States, make up the world's three largest holders of nuclear weapons.
But a range of other global challenges are lingering in the background, including the war in Iran and tensions over trade and artificial intelligence...

item.title: [Guardian China] Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
item.description:
The Markley Lowell datacentre in Lowell, Massachusetts. The US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. Photograph: Lauren Owens Lambert/AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
The Markley Lowell datacentre in Lowell, Massachusetts. The US is expected to rely on gas to provide about 60% of the electricity for its datacentres by 2030. Photograph: Lauren Owens Lambert/AFP/Getty Images
Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas
The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.
The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
The Paris-based agency found that the breakneck pace of the industry’s growth means that within four years AI datacentres will consume an extra 350 terrawatt-hours of electricity every year, or more than the annual electricity consumption of Great Britain.
Its influential annual report warned that the world’s energy future was less certain after the impact of the Middle East war, which it has described as the greatest energy market disruption in history.
“I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” said the IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol.
Instead, it will be reshaped by the policy decisions governments make after the crisis to meet the increasing demand for energy to power a growing global population, the rising need for air-conditioning and a booming AI economy, the IEA said.

item.title: [BBC World] This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are meeting for a historic trilateral summitByLaura BickerChina correspondent , Reporting fromShenzhenPublished3 hours ago
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Follow live updates: Trump, Xi and Putin hold historic meeting on Apec sidelines
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's fu...

item.description:
Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef
View image in fullscreen
Seven countries in Africa expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Photograph: Frank Dejongh/Unicef
One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds
One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”

Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.
The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.

The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Apec’s Chinese hosts went out of their way to give world leaders a warm welcome as they arrived in Shenzhen this week. Military bands played, dozens of cheering young men and women waved colourful bouquets, and senior officials offered hugs and handshakes on the tarmac.

item.title: [NPR News] Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
item.description:
Technology
Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
November 18, 20266:54 PM ET
John Ruwitch
Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty Images
The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic said in a statement that "certain stockholders" also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO, bringing the total haul to more than $81.3 billion.

item.description:
Brazil's Senate approves Lula's $10 billion fiscal package after costly election spending
Brazil’s Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late OctoberByMAURICIO SAVARESE Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 5:56 PM
SAO PAULO -- SAO PAULO (AP) — Brazil 's Senate approved on Wednesday a plan by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva to control his government’s spending and increase revenues after his reelection late October led market analysts to worry about Brazil’s economy. The 81-year-old leader came back with a series of incentives to voters after losing the first round of voting to Flávio Bolsonaro.
The Brazilian government’s fiscal package, which will also have to be approved by the lower house, introduces new rules to slow down the growth of spending, limits corporate tax breaks and closes loopholes. It seeks to improve the ‌public finances by up to 60 billion reais (about $10 billion) next year.
Lula’s move is laying bare the challenges ahead of his fourth nonconsecutive administration, as it already has many critics left and right. Many of his supporters see the plan as a risk to welfare programs, while his critics among market agents deem it to be too shy.
Many analysts say Lula's fiscal package is too dependent on boosting revenues rather than cutting expenses. That perception has led to the depreciation of Brazilian assets in recent days, including the country's real currency. Lula is yet to announce who will be his finance minister for the new term.
Lula’s victories in 2002 and 2022 also sparked immediate depreciation of Brazilian assets, but stock markets eventually recovered from high losses.
Ahead of the runoff election, Lula rolled out costly initiatives, including a 15% increase in his flagship welfare program Bolsa Família, or Family Grant. That measure alone will cost 5.8 billion reais ($1 billion) this year and arou...

item.title: [BBC World] Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
item.description:
Image source, Getty ImagesByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentPublished9 hours ago
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.
In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.
But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."
The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.
I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.
Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.
I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.
But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff. It wasn’t immediately clear if he was killed.
Bukele posted a video on X that depicts an old video of Jeff posing in front of his mansion in the Caribbean country and then cuts to Salvadoran helicopters flying toward it as they fire shot after shot, with big plumes of smoke rising from Jeff’s home.
“My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières,” Bukele wrote.
The 1803 battle was critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France and transforming it into the world's first Black republic.
It wasn’t immediately known if Haiti’s police and army were involved. A U.N.-backed gang suppression force said that it wasn’t involved.
Jeff is considered one of Haiti's most powerful gang leaders. His real name is Jeff Larose, but he's known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa and Taliban. He has long controlled a community known as Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince, leading a gang of an estimated 200 members, according to the United Nations. His so-called Taliban gang based in Canaan is a very close ally of 5 Segond, which has provided it with reinforcements.
Diego Da Rin, a Haiti expert with International Crisis Group, said the attack on Jeff’s home was the obvious next step for Bukele’s operations.
Jeff built the home in mid-2024, complete with a pool emblazoned with his logo.

item.title: [ABC News World] A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
item.description:
A Chinese executive is convicted in a case linked to a Bangkok building collapse
A Thai court has found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders guilty of illegally operating a business in ThailandByJINTAMAS SAKSORNCHAI Associated PressNovember 18, 2026, 10:56 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BANGKOK -- A court in Thailand on Wednesday found a Chinese executive and Thai shareholders of a Thai subsidiary of a Chinese state-owned construction company guilty of illegally operating a business in Thailand in a case related to the collapse of a Bangkok office building last year.
At least 92 people died on March 28, 2025, when an earthquake struck the partially built high-rise, which was to house the State Audit Office. It was the only building in Thailand to collapse completely due to the 7.7-magnitude quake, which was centered in neighboring Myanmar.
The tower was being built by a joint venture between China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and Italian-Thai Development. Executives from both companies are also facing separate proceedings over alleged wrongdoing related to the building’s collapse.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) and its director, Zhang Chuanling, were found guilty of violating Thailand’s Foreign Business Act by using Thai nominee shareholders to conceal the company’s foreign ownership and operating a construction business without the required permission. The Criminal Court in Bangkok fined the company and Zhang 1 million baht ($29,450) each and sentenced Zhang to three years in prison, while also ordering the company to cease operations.
The defendants had denied the charges and were granted bail.
China Railway No. 10 (Thailand) is a Thai-registered affiliate of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group, part of the Chinese state-owned China Railway group, which operates internationally.

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. item.title: [BBC China] As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal

Image source, Getty ImagesByLaura BickerChina correspondentPublished17 November 2026
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become some...

item.title: [BBC China] How new US chip restrictions on South East Asia will hit China
item.description:
Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
Xi and Trump when they met in Beijing in MayByOsmond ChiaBusiness reporterPublished17 November 2026
As US President Donald Trump heads to China, his administration has renewed efforts to curb Beijing's access to advanced semiconductors.
On Monday, Washington announced new interim rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.
The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models.
South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market.
But now these firms will need a US government licence to buy advanced chips from Nvidia or other American chipmakers. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China.
This poses a fresh challenge for Beijing, which has become deeply dependent on compute from abroad in the wake of US export restrictions. At least 30% of China's advanced AI computing power is projected to come from renting overseas or smuggling in 2027, according to research by the Institute for Progress, external, a US-based think-tank.
China's foreign ministry called the new rules "economic coercion" and said Beijing "will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its own legitimate rights and interests".
A blow to Asia's AI boom
This is also a problem for South East Asian economies where large numbers of data centres have sprung up recently. Some of the firms behind them are accused of helping China evade US export controls on advanced chips.
